facts.text: Occlusion means an object is hidden behind something else so a sensor cannot see it; sensor obstruction means the sensor itself is blocked, for example by mud on its window.
facts.quote: Occlusion is when an object is hidden behind something else so the sensor cannot see it, and obstruction is when the sensor itself is blocked, for example by mud on its window.

facts.text: Heavy machines can occlude their own sensors when booms, buckets and dump bodies swing into the field of view.
facts.quote: Heavy machines occlude themselves: booms, buckets and dump bodies swing into the field of view

facts.text: ISO 21815-3 excludes machine heights beyond the travel position from its scope.
facts.quote: ISO 21815-3, the international standard for this function, notes that machine heights beyond the travel position are out of its scope [Chapter 6].

facts.text: Ground-truth labeling rules must specify whether a partially hidden person counts as a detection opportunity.

facts.text: The ground-truth reference system needs a “truth unavailable or ambiguous” state to prevent occlusion and dust from being forced into wrong labels.

facts.text: In virtual sites, a sensor cannot recover surfaces it never saw; gaps filled visually by neural methods should not silently become geometric truth.

facts.text: Camera soiling is simulated using overlays whose realism is judged by eye rather than by measured light transmission.

facts.text: Occlusion and sensor obstruction can both leave a person unseen, but require different remedies: occlusion needs sensor placement, prediction and cautious logic, while obstruction needs self-diagnosis, cleaning and a safe degraded mode.

facts.text: The booklet recommends concentrating failure-seeking tests on partial visibility and sensor degradation.
